title: Recording the Benny Goodman session in 1939
summary: Bass on Goodman's last Victor date.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: You recorded with Benny?
I recorded with Benny, yeah, when he was here. I remember how bad he was. He was kind of funny. His brother was playing bass fiddle with him then.
Yeah, who was that?
His name was Goodman, too. (Harry)

Let's see, the trumpet player, he (Goodman) was Irving. / Yeah, and then the other brother was playing bass. In fact, Teddy Wilson told me that's why the trio was a trio, and not a quartet. Because they really didn't make it on bass.

Yeah, the bass player. So Lionel knew about me as he was raised here in Chicago. So he recognized me as being good, and I made that session one time, for old Victor. On Lakeshore Drive, right there at the S-curve.
Yeah, by the Drake Hotel?
No, it was on the outer drive, just before you go into that big grey building over on the east side of the Drive, just before you get to the S-curve?
Oh, yeah.
Going south? That's where Victor used to be.
I see. Well, about when was that?
It must have been around 1939, later, after I'd left Earl. Must have been in the forties.
Well, was Hamp still with Goodman then?
Yeah. Hamp was still with him, and let's see, Ziggy Elman (PHONETIC) was with him, Harry James, and -- I'm trying to think of the tenor players. That was the old Benny Goodman band.
Bud Freeman was with him for a while.
Yeah, Bud Freeman.
Arthur Rollini, I believe, was with him.
Yeah.
That must have been earlier than 1940, because a lot of those guys had left about '38, '39, somewhere in there.
Well, I know this was -- I hadn't been working. And I wasn't with Earl then, I don't think.
Well, do you remember what you recorded with Benny?
No, I can't. I'm trying to think of the name of that tune we recorded with Ziggy Elman.
Under Ziggy's name?
No, under Benny's name. He did the feature trumpet, like that Jewish thing he did.
Oh, yeah, like in 'The Angels Sing.'
It wasn't 'The Angels Sing,' it was another one he did.
Have you gotten credit for this in
I don't know. I don't think so.
I don't think so, either.
I don't think so, either. I'm not listed in any of that stuff.
But you did do this --
Yeah, I did do that. I remember doing that session, one session.
About how many tunes were recorded, do you remember?
Oh, about four tunes.
Four tunes. That's a pretty standard --
Yeah, that was pretty standard back then.
Gee, it would be nice to know at least one of the titles.
Just like I say, when I was recording, I never paid too much attention to titles. A lot of that stuff I never figured would be history, you know.
(Recording interruption.)
Interviewer's insert: The session that Quinn talks about, Benny Goodman session, research, it was May 4th, 1939. It was Goodman's last Victor recording session before he went with Columbia.

The tune that he mentions that Ziggy Elman played on, or was featured on, was "Who Will Buy My Bublikhki". The other two tunes on the session were, the big band version of "Pick a Rib," and "You and Your Love," which had a vocal by Martha Tilton.

Russ Connors' Biodiscography of Goodman does not have this information, except that it mentions that it's possible that Quinn Wilson was the bass player. So Quinn has confirmed that he was the bass player. This information has been sent to Russ Connors for whatever purposes he cares to make of it.
